::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The short version
- This course is the operating manual for getting software changes into production at a blood
  center: in-house releases, vendor BECS upgrades, and emergency fixes.
- Earlier courses taught *what* validation and change control are. This one teaches *how* releases
  actually move: lifecycle models, requirements, environments, release planning, testing,
  pipelines, secure development, cutover, rollback, hotfixes and metrics.
- The running example is Lakeshore's own Hospital Ordering Portal and its 3.0 release, the BECS
  vendor's Release C, and one very bad night with a critical vulnerability.
- Every module ends with what a regulator, an assessor and your CIO would each expect to see.
:::

## The finish line

By the end of this course you can run any software change at Lakeshore — an in-house release, a
vendor's BECS (blood establishment computer software) upgrade, or a 2 a.m. security hotfix — from
idea to production and back out again if needed, and say at every step what evidence a regulator,
an assessor, and your own CIO would expect to see.

## Why this course exists

You already know release management from the ITSM side. What changes in a blood center is that a
release can put the wrong unit on a shelf or the wrong label on a bag, so every step leaves
evidence that someone outside IT will one day read. The earlier courses built the vocabulary:
[CSV & BECS](../csv-and-becs/index.qmd) taught validation, the V-model and the validated state;
[Quality System Essentials](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd) taught change control; and
[ITSM for Regulated Blood Services](../itsm-for-regulated-blood-services/index.qmd) mapped ITIL's
change enablement onto it. This course doesn't repeat any of that. It puts it to work on real
releases, and adds the modern practice those courses only touched: agile, automated pipelines,
secure development and software supply chains.

## The eleven modules

1. **SDLC models in a regulated blood center.** Waterfall, V-model, iterative, agile and DevOps:
   what each one has to produce for validation, and when. HOP 3.0's auto-allocation feature raises
   the question of whether in-house software can drift into being a BECS.
2. **Requirements, backlogs and traceability in agile.** Turning user stories into requirements an
   inspector can trace to tests, and a definition of done that includes the validation evidence.
3. **Environments, baselines and test data.** Development, test, validation and production; keeping
   a configuration baseline; keeping real donor data out of places it shouldn't be.
4. **Release management, deployment and change control.** Three ITIL practices that get blurred
   together, release types, and a release calendar that respects blood operations.
5. **Vendor release intake for BECS.** Taking the vendor's Release C from release notes to a
   validation-in-your-facility decision.
6. **Risk-based testing and regression.** Sizing a test effort by risk and deciding regression
   scope from an impact analysis.
7. **CI/CD pipelines under GxP.** Automation without losing segregation of duties, tool assurance,
   or the record of who deployed what.
8. **Secure SDLC and software supply chain.** NIST's Secure Software Development Framework applied
   to HOP, and the supply-chain questions to ask a vendor.
9. **Deployment, cutover and rollback.** Go/no-go, BECS downtime procedures, post-deployment
   verification, and a rollback you've actually rehearsed.
10. **Emergency changes and hotfixes.** Shipping a critical fix fast without leaving a validation
    gap.
11. **Post-release review and delivery metrics.** Hypercare, post-implementation review, and the
    delivery metrics worth reporting upward.
